items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have pleasure in informing the House that a parliamentary
delegation from the Legislative Assembly of Queensland, led by Mr Kerry Shine MP,
Chairperson of the Industry, Education, Training and Industrial Relations Committee, is
present in the gallery. I am sure members would wish that that delegation be welcomed.
Youth Suicide—Kawerau Core Clinical Committee
1. RAHUI KATENE (M āori Party—Te Tai Tonga)  to the Associate Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: When was the Core Clinical Committee established in Kawerau and how are
iwi involved in the membership and functions of this joint taskforce to tackle youth
suicide?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The Core Clinical
Committee was established in the wake of a number of tragic suicides in Kawerau in
2010 and 2011. It includes a range of organisa tions designed to provide a cross-agency
platform for response. The organisations i nvolved include Kia Piki  o te Ora, and iwi
groups such as Ng āti T ūwharetoa, T ūwharetoa ki Kawarau Hauora Trust, and T ūhoe
Hauora Trust, as well as the police, mental  health services, Child, Youth and Family,
the Ministry of Youth Development, local colleges, and Victim Support.

items.speaker: Rahui Katene
items.text: What resourcing is available to directly assist families in Kawerau
who have suffered over 14 deaths of their young people over the last 18 months?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Clinical Advisory Services Ao tearoa is contracted through
the Ministry of Health to provide postv ention services, and doe s this through its
community postvention response service. The service is actively working in the area,
along with the local Kia Piki provider, Toi te Ora, and I understand that the Ministry of
Education has also put resources into local schools. In addition, a group of key agencies,
including community agencies, meets regularly to screen those affected by the suicides
and to provide support within the college to the young people who are living with the
consequences. Mana Social Services Tr ust has seen a number of youths and wh ānau,
following recent tragic events.

items.speaker: Rahui Katene
items.text: How many of the suicides identified in Kawerau are young M āori,
and what approach has he made to ensure wh ānau have access to Te Whakauruora,
which is a community action - focuse d resource to build  capacity in M āori suicide
prevention?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: There are believed to have been between nine and 12
suspected suicides in Kawerau in 2010 and 2011, and a further four attempted suicides.
Almost all of the suspected and attempte d cases are of young people 14 to 18 years old,
and they are predominantly M āori and male. In response to  the second part of the
member’s question, I am not aware of whethe r Te Whakauruora has been used in this
specific situation, but I encourage its use, and I will certainly be following up with
officials over its availability to the wider Kawerau community.
19588 Questions for Oral Answer 22 Jun 2011
Infrastructure Programme, Investment—Progress
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Infrastructure
items.text: What progress is the Governme nt making on its infrastructure
investment programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is making very good
progress. The Government laid  out a programme 2½ years a go, and despite the fact of
the recession and significant Government deficits, we have actually held our capital
spending and increased investment in infrastructure, because we believe that in the long
run, investment in productive infrastructure will help our export se ctor to be more
competitive, and will therefore help to rebalance this economy. In addition to this
spending, we have changed the rules on consen ting for infrastructure projects so that
they can occur much more quickly than in the past.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How has the Government’s infrastructure programme supported
jobs?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One of the benefits of th is long-term investment in
infrastructure happened to be that during the recession, when we were ramping up the
programme, the Government’s infrastructure spend directly supported thousands of jobs
across New Zealand in the c onstruction sector, which, as we know, was hit very hard,
both by the New Zealand recession and then by the effects of the global recession. A
very significant proportion of  all non-residential building in New Zealand has been
funded over the last 2 or 3 years as part of  the Government infrastructure investment
programme.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What are the Government’s infrastructure spending plans for the
next 5 years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is just more good news. We expect to invest heavily in
what is now a clearly defined pipeline of work. Over the next 5 years we will invest
$750 million in KiwiRail for new wagons, loco motives, and other projects to increase
productivity, and $5.4 billion in  new State highways, which will mean the start of
construction of the Waterview Connection, four more sections of the Waikato
Expressway, and the MacKays Crossing to Peka Peka Road  part of State Highway 1.
We will be spending $3.9 billion on upgrading the national electricity grid and spending
$7 billion on State housing, schools, hospitals, and the prison system. Of course there is
also the investment of at le ast $1.5 billion in the roll-out  of ultra-fast broadband, for
which the final commercial arrangements have been put in place in just the last few
weeks. Parliament will pass that legislation hopefully in the next few weeks.

items.speaker: Hon John Boscawen
items.text: How does the Government intend to attract private capital to
boost New Zealand’s infrastructure base?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has taken a careful and considerate
approach to introducing public-private part nerships, being one of the few developed
countries in the world that has not had those in place in the last 10 years. We have learnt
from others, and we are making cautious progress in that respect.

items.speaker: Hon John Boscawen
items.text: Would he describe the comme nt made by the Hon Trevor
Mallard regarding broadband infrastructure investment that “Anyone entering into an
arrangement based on this legislation has go t to know that it may not last,” as being
wanton economic thuggery that wo uld scare away private infrastructure investment and
turn New Zealand into a banana republic; if not, how would he describe it?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Although that is
som
ething that I might like to frame and se nd to my Labour electorate committee, I
think asking the Minister of Finance to ha ve responsibility for my comment is going a
little bit far.
22 Jun 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 19589

items.speaker: Hon John Boscawen
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not need to hear further on the matter. The Minister certainly
does not have responsibility for the honourable member’s comment, but Ministers can
be asked their opinions on all sorts of thi ngs. As long as the Minister is somewhat
careful in answering it, I am prepared to allow the question, but certainly the Minister
has no responsibility for that comment.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I do not think the
member had finished. It was such a good quote, I would like—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member had finished.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think it is more bark than bite, because, firstly, no New
Zealand Government would act illegally and it would comply with the contract;
secondly, that comment is reckless; and, thirdly, I will work very hard over the next few
months to make sure that the election of 2011 makes that comment irrelevant.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: If his stated aim of infrastruc ture investment is to boost our
economy through streamlining private sector exports, then why are poorly maintained
rural roads being ripped up by milk tank ers while his Associate Minister for
Infrastructure, Steven Joyce, squanders $1.8 billion on the Holiday Highway, which has
a benefit-cost ratio of just 80c in the dollar?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am most impressed with this newfound sympathy of the
Labour Party for the farming community, but those members need to sort out their
strategy, because last week they were kicki ng farmers in the slats and today they are
trying to hug them. As someone who lives on one of those poorly maintained rural
roads, I say that the Government has done  a very good job of working with local
government to make sure the rural infrastruc ture can support the very successful export
efforts of our rural sector.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Can he confirm that land transport funding will be reallocated
later this year by the new G overnment policy statement, with more money being taken
out of road safety, maintenance, and public transport and instead  being funnelled into
four new so-called roads of national significance, which will, presumably, have even
worse benefit-cost ratios than the road from Pūhoi to Wellsford?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I cannot confirm that. I can confirm that the process of
allocation is arm’s length and very focused on productivity, so much so that the most
recent tar-sealing programme in Dipton actually  stops at the end of English Road. We
have the same gravel road that we have had for 100 years. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The members’ colleague has called for a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I just ask whether the
Minister might repeat his an swer. It was very difficult to  hear, and I am an “English
patient”.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I think the member heard the answer perfectly well.
Pike River Mine Safety—Prime Minister’s Statements
3. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
What advice did he rely on when commenti ng in Australia on the safety of the Pike
River coalmine?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I did not provide a view on the safety of the
Pike River coalmine; I pointed  out its design and the diffe rences I understood there
were with Australian mines. For the purposes of clarification, let me read out the actual
transcript of what I said. The questi on asked by Dennis Shanahan from the  Australian
was the following: “The issue of mining sa fe ty in New Zealand seems to be behind
Australia’s. Do you accept that ?”. My answer was: “I don’t  think I’m in a position to
fully give you a view on that, but what I can  say is that there’s a royal commission of
19590 Questions for Oral Answer 22 Jun 2011
inquiry into the Pike River mine disaster. On that commission is Stuart Bell from
Australia, who’s one of the major mine experts here in Australia.  I do think, rightfully
so, we need to ask some questions whether mine safety standards are high enough.
What is true is that the Pike River mine c ouldn’t have been constructed in that way in
Australia. The single entry, 2.4km, upwards-slo ping mine shaft, I don’t believe, is legal
in Australia and so from New Zealand’s point of view we ha ve to ensure we have the
world’s best practice. I have no doubt that there will be changes actually recommended
in New Zealand. We’ve taken an interim revi ew of our mines to check the safety, but
long term there’ll need to be other changes, I suspect.”

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did he criticise a union delegate for talking about the
safety of the Pike River mine before th e royal commission of inquiry was completed,
but he felt able to answer a question by an Australian media person about mines and
mine safety in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because if I had done that and had talked about mine safety, I
would have been hypocritical, but  I did not; I talked about th e construction of the mine
and the differences between New Zealand and Australia. I would add that it was a mine
that was consented under a Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I think you need to tell
that member that 1998 was a National—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will resume his seat immediately. That is an outright
abuse of the point of order pr ocess. The shadow Leader of the House should set a better
example. He may not agree with the Prime Mi nister’s answer, but he should not use the
point of order process to voice his disagreement. He should be careful of doing that.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Was that mine first consented in 1998?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not in a position to confirm that.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can I draw your
attention—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the member cannot. The Prim e Minister has answered two
questions in the way he sees fit. As long as  the question has been answered and nothing
unparliamentary has been said, it is not up to  the Speaker to adjudicate on the accuracy
or otherwise of any answer. That is not the way question time is conducted.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Which answer was correct: his answer to Annette King’s
supplementary question or his answer to mine?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Both.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If he is now saying that mine  safety standards need to be
changed, why wait until after the royal comm ission has reported to make the changes,
or is he prepared to guarantee that no furthe r mining accidents will happen in the next 2
years under the current mining regulations?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not saying that they need to change; I have said, exactly,
that the royal commission of inquiry needs to look at that matter. I have simply made
the point that a particular mine that was c onstructed in New Zealand would not be legal
to be constructed in Australia.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: As an interim measure until th e royal commission reports, will
he implement the Queensland regulatory standards for mine safety, which are
considered world best practice, and will he contract experts from Queensland to come to
New Zealand to oversee their implementation; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, because an audit was taken of the safety of mines. We are
now working our way through the royal commi ssion of inquiry, and w e will see what
recommendations it makes.
22 Jun 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 19591

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that family members of Pike River miners are now
calling for increased mine inspection to occur now; if not, why not li sten to what they
have to say, rather than wait?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because we have undertaken a safety audit of New Zealand
mines and we are now waiting for the royal commission to make recommendations.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did his Government halt th e review of mine safety in

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member would have to direct that question to the
appropriate Minister, who is the best person to answer that question. I can say, from the
top of my head, that there were a number of factors in relation to smaller mines.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Can he confirm that generic occupational safety and health
regulations leave the ultimate responsibility for mine plans to the mine manager?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. That question would have to be directed to the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: When was the Pike River mine first consented?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know the answer to that question.
Earthquakes, Canterbury—Support Provided by Department of Corrections
4. NICKY WAGNER (National) to the Minister of Corrections: What support has
the Corrections Department provided in Cant erbury since the first earthquake struck in
September last year?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I am very pleased to advise
that since the first earthquake in Septembe r last year, offenders on community work
have provided over 170,000 hours of free labour to help to clean up Christchurch.
Offenders on community work have been used to clear streets, assist in getting schools
and early childhood centres b ack up and running, and tidy up parks, reserves, and
marae. Following last week’s aftershocks, offenders on community work were quickly
sent out to the eastern suburbs, where th ey have helped non- profit organisations,
community groups, and others to clear the s ilt and liquefaction from their properties.
The department will continue to ensure that offenders on community work are available
to help out in the months ahead.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What actions have the department  and staff taken to support their
colleagues in Christchurch?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: From today, Christchurch-based corrections staff will be
receiving the benefit of the department’s Give your Mates a Day Trust. The trust was set
up after February’s earthquake, and nearly  1,000 staff from around the country have
kindly donated a day of their leave. The department put the net dollar value of that leave
in a trust. Due to the generosity and goodwill of staff, a total of $166,430 has been
raised. This money is now being distributed  to Christchurch corrections staff, and
payments will be completed by this Friday.
Government Contracts—Use of Kiwi Companies
5. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : Does he believe
that in the current economic environmen t kiwi companies should be considered
favourably with regards to big government contracts?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I believe the current economic
environment makes it even more important th at Government spending achieves the best
value for money possible on behalf of taxpayers. In that respect we are simply following
the guidelines that the previ ous Labour Governm ent laid down in 2007. I quote: “New
Zealand’s own government procurement market is open and competitive, and the policy
does not call for discrimination against foreign suppliers.”
19592 Questions for Oral Answer 22 Jun 2011

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Have members of his Government vowed that the multimillion-
dollar contracts to build thousands of temporary houses and utility blocks in
Christchurch will go to Kiwi companies, and does he agree?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I have not heard su ch vows being made. The
Government has been exploring the market for temporary housing, and some results of
that will be coming back in pretty soon, I think.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he believe that preference should be given to New Zealand
companies in the building of thousands of temporary homes in Christchurch?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I believe preference should be given to the people of
Christchurch being able to get access as quickly as is necessary to a reasonable quality
of temporary housing, and that is what the Government processes aim to do.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Will the Government release a cost-benefit analysis as to the
benefits of those houses being built by New Zealand companies rather than overseas
contractors?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That might be an interesting idea; I am not sure what it
would show. We have been focusing more on the needs of the people of Christchurch,
some of whom need temporary accommodation, and we will continue to do so.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Given the significant size of th e flat-deck wagon contract with
KiwiRail and the implications for New Zeal and’s rail engineering workforce, will he
commission a report into the real cost difference, if a ny, between imported flat-deck
wagons and New Zealand - built ones?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As has been discussed in th e House, decisions about that
issue were made on a commercial basis by the KiwiRail board. The Government needs
to give KiwiRail the best possible opportunity to be a successful and viable
organisation. As I think ev eryone knows, that is quite a challenge. It needs every
advantage we can give it.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Does he deny that a senior KiwiRa il representative said at a meeting
of KiwiRail’s mechanical council committee on  23 March that a political decision had
been made to buy the 3,700 flat-deck wagons  from outside New Z ealand, rather than
have them built in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have no idea what transpired at that meeting, but if anyone
said that, they would certainly have been wrong.
Parents, First-time—Support
6. TIM MACINDOE (National—Hamilton West)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development and Employment
items.text: What parenting support is being made available for
first-time parents?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.role: Minister for So cial Development and Employment

items.text: Last year 63,000 babies were born in New Zealand. Raising Children in New Zealand is
a new parenting DVD, which will be launched at Parliament this evening. In partnership
with the Lion Foundation, Barnardos, Plunke t, and Television Ne w Zealand, we are
helping first-time mums and dads get quality advice on raising their newborn babies.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What other initiatives for parents is the Government supporting?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: This DVD is just one of a range of initiatives that this
Government is putting investment in for new parents and families. Many of the
initiatives have come from the Minister of Health and have been very well received out
there. In my own area, every year we spend around $50 million on parenting support.
Under this Budget we saw an expansion of  the HIPPY (Home Interaction Programme
for Parents and Youngsters) under the Minister of Education, $2.4 million for parenting
support for foster carers
and grandparents raising grandchildren, $21.3 million for Well
22 Jun 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 19593
Child services, and more than $550 million for early childhood education. This
Government, in a small way, is providing that sort of support for parents.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I seek leave of the House
to table the consents for the Pike River mine that were issued on 23 May 2003, and the

Tax System Changes—Effect on New Zealanders
7. Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South)  to the Prime Minister: In
light of the answer given on his behalf to  Oral Question No 2 on 15 June, is it his
opinion that real average after-tax wages do not go up when high-income earners get tax
cuts and low-income workers lose their jobs?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is my opinion that real after-tax wages go
up when the economy becomes more productive and people get to keep more of the
money that they earn. That is why the real after-tax wage has gone up by 10 percent
since 2008, but went up by only 4 percent ove r the 9 years before that under a Labour
Government.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: What does happen to average net after-tax wages when high-
income earners get tax cuts?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That would be subject to, and depend on, a number of factors.
It is not possible to say immediately, because it would depend on, amongst other things,
the inflation rate, the number of people w ho are working, and various other component
parts.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I seek leave to table a docum ent that was prepared by the
Parliamentary Library, which shows the incr ease in average wages as a result of the
National Government’s tax cuts for the rich.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Oh, they don’t like the truth.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There is objection, because of the way the document was described.
[Interruption] The reason why there was objection, I su spect, relates to the last words
used in the seeking of leave.
Border Control—Joint Border Management System

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: My question is to the Minister of Customs: what recent
reports has he received—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise to Paul Quinn, whose voice is not lacking in volume at
all. But with the interjections that were going across the front of the House I was
struggling to hear even Mr Quinn, which is quite extraordinary. With those interjections
now ceased, please, Paul Quinn on question No. 8.
8. PAUL QUINN (National)  to the Minister of Customs: What recent reports has
he received on developments to technology at the border?
19594 Questions for Oral Answer 22 Jun 2011

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I bring more great
tidings of joy to this House. The New Z ealand Customs Service last week signed an
agreement with IBM that will start the development of a Joint Border Management
System, or JBMS. It will bring together the two border processing systems that were
previously run independently by the New Zealand Customs Service and by the Ministry
of Agriculture and Forestry. A $75 million a ppropriation will cover the first stage of the
Joint Border Management System development. Stage one will include what is called
the trade single window, which will enable expo rters, importers and others involved in
trade to complete all their border compliance requirements online through a single point
of electronic contact.

items.speaker: Paul Quinn
items.text: What benefits will the Joint Border  Management System bring to the
border?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Bringing these two previously independent
systems together will give us more efficien cy, allowing for more effective trade, and
will improve biosecurity. The Joint Border Management System is designed to
significantly improve border processing for New Zealand importers and exporters, and
to make the border agencies more effective. The Joint Border Management System will
move the agencies away from fragmented, separate processes that result in a duplication
of efforts to a far more cohesive system that shares processes,  data, and technology
between border agencies and between industries.
Budget 2011—Vote Health Allocation
9. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: Has sufficient funding been allocated in  Vote Health to meet the increasing
costs facing organisations working in the health sector?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: There are 40,000-plus contracts funded
by the Ministry of Health and the district health boards. These include
telecommunications, building, medical suppli es, and health services. Each faces
different cost pressures. However, I do know that Vote Health has once again been the
recipient of the biggest amount  of new money from the Budget. That money is flowing
through the Ministry of Health and the district health boards to other providers that they
contract with.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Given previous answers by the Minister last week, can he
confirm that the funding alloca ted in Budget 2011 to the district health boards does not
meet inflation costs in the health sector?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: It is too early to give a defi nitive answer to that question,
because the district health boards will receive additional funding through the year
related to various projects and contracts.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has he read the article in the Bay of Plenty Times  under the
headline “Health services on the brink”, whic h shows that agencies such as Arthritis
New Zealand are unable to provide services in his own community?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL

Mine Safety—Underground Coalmines
10. KEVIN HAGUE (Green)  to the Minister of Labour: Was she satisfied before
the first explosion in the Pike River coal  mine, that her Government had done all it
could to ensure the workplace  safety of people working in  underground coal mines; if
so, why?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: According to advice received, I
had no reason to believe that the hazards in underground coalmines were not being
managed. Immediately after the tragedy at Pike River the Government commissioned an
independent safety audit of all other underground mines, which recommended a number
of safety improvements in those mines but reported that there was no evidence that a
dangerous situation was imminent. We have also established a royal commission of
inquiry with very wide terms of reference to inquire into all aspects of the explosion and
mine safety.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: What steps has she taken to impl ement the call for the reinstatement
of check inspectors in the 2008 Department of Labour  discussion paper aimed at
improving the health and safety in the underground mining industry?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: The advice I received at the time was that check
inspectors would not necessarily  improve mine safety, as the legal responsibility in our
legislation needs to be squarely on employers.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Why has the Minister ruled out th e reinstitution of worker-appointed
mine check inspectors, abolished by the National Government in 1992?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I have not ruled that out; in  fact, it will be one of the
issues that the royal commission of inquiry will look at, and we will be taking those
recommendations very seriously and acting accordingly.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Is she aware that Australia still uses check inspectors, and what has
she instructed her department  to do to learn from health  and safety standards in
Australian underground mining?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I understand that in some st ates in Australia they use
check inspectors; in other states they do not use check inspectors.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Why will the Minister not now reinstate the mines inspectorate,
dismantled by the National Government in 1998, in light of her department’s May 2011
report slamming the current system of mines inspection?
19596 Questions for Oral Answer 22 Jun 2011

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Because we are waiting for the recommendations of the
royal commission of inquiry, which will be giving a comprehensive review of the mines
and the legislation relating thereto.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: In light of the Pike River mine  disaster, does she agree with the
reassurance of the Hon Max Bradford in 1998 that changes to the mines inspectorate
would not downgrade mine safety, or with Mr Peter Ewen, the author of the book

items.speaker: Strongman
items.text: Three Score and More, who says: “The wisdom of the inspectorate changes
in 1998 has been questioned by numerous parties, and unfortunately it will only be a
matter of when, not if, several pay with their lives, given the ill-considered changes to
the inspector’s role. Ministerial condolences that will follow will be of small comfort to
the bereaved.”?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I think we can all agree that a very real and serious
tragedy happened on Pike River. That is why we have taken the matter seriously. We
have an internal investigation, we have a health and safety in employment investigation,
and we have a royal comm ission of inquiry, because, like everybody else in New
Zealand, we want to know exactly what happened and why it happened, and we want to
prevent it happening again.

items.text: Why did the Government halt the review of mine safety in 2009?

items.text: The review was not halted by me. In fact, some of the

asked.

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON

items.text: Why did she not open a review or take seriously the requests

items.text: Why did she not reopen the review in May 2010 when

items.text: We had a review of small mines, I took that review very

items.text: Does she agree that the Government  has a share of the responsibility

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I point out to that member that a fundamental premise
of heath and safety in employment legislation is that the primary responsibility for

Western Hoki Fishery—Recovery of Stocks
11. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister of Fisheries and

items.speaker: Aquaculture
items.text: What recent announcement has he made about the recovery of the
western hoki stock?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Today I
announced the recovery of the western hoki stock following a period of low recruitment,
which saw stocks depleted between 2003 and 2006. The Ministry of Fisheries and the
industry worked together to make large reduc tions in catch. It is a move that has now
paid off, with the scientific evidence meani ng that the ministry is able to declare the
19598 Questions for Oral Answer 22 Jun 2011
stock rebuilt. This may allow for the reconsideration of total allowable catches later this
year. This is exactly how the quota management system should work.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: How is the management of New Zeal and’s fisheries stock regarded by
scientists internationally?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: We manage our fisheries resources through an ongoing
process of review and adjustment. New Z ealand’s success in this area was recently
documented in a report, “Rebuilding Global Fisheries”, which wa s co-authored by 20
international fisheries and marine scientists, and New Zealand came right at the top.
Minimum Wage—Minister’s Statements
12. DARIEN FENTON (Labour) to the Minister of Labour: Does she stand by all
her answers to Oral Question No 10 yesterday?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Does she stand by her statement that “We are aware that for those
people on the minimum wage, budgeting is tight.”; if so, does she support increasing the
minimum wage to $15 an hour to make it easier for minimum-wage workers who are
facing tight budgets?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Yes, to the first part of that question. To the second part
of that question, although we would all like a high minimum wage—and even $15 an
hour is a high minimum wage—if it results in the loss of 6,000 jobs, then we do not
think that that is a very helpful, supportive, or practical solution for those young people
who are trying to get employment.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Was her comment “If you’ve got somebody who is 16 who is
wanting a job and someone who is 30 at the same price, then who is the employer going
to employ?” an admission that a youth mi nimum wage will shift the issue of
unemployment from one group to another?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes; to the
second part, no.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business . Yesterday in Parliament the Prime Minister, in reply to
a question, reluctantly admitted there was “a degree of inequality in New Zealand,”—a
degree of inequality. But he does not believ e we are a deeply une qual country, and he
does not think we are as bad as others. Well, I have to say to the Prime Minister and the
National Government that they are badly out  of touch with what is going on in this
country today. They have become blinkere d. The Prime Minister is basking in the
adoration he receives from people around New Zealand, Government members are
believing their own propaganda, and together they are blinded by their own “brilliance”.
But I have to tell them that inequality is growing in New Zealand at an alarming rate.

items.speaker: Paul Quinn
items.text: Brilliance. That’s it—brilliance!

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I suggest that Mr Quinn takes off the blinkers, stops
looking at his own “brilliance”, and has a look at what is happening around New
Zealand. There is an alarming rate of growth  in inequality in this country. But do we
think this Government will listen? Does it care? Will it do anything about it? The
answer to those questions has to be “No”. Over the last 6 months I have taken time to go
out and visit a few regions around New Zealand, and I come back to this House to
report on what is happening. There are four re gions I will talk about today. What is
really happening, on the ground, to New Zealanders  in this country th at is only a little
bit unequal?
22 Jun 2011 General Debate 19599
I will first go to Invercargi ll. In Invercargill I visited the Salvation Army food bank
and the budgeting services there. What did pe ople tell me? The message I heard up and
down New Zealand was that there has been a huge growth in peopl e having to go to
food banks. Are they our usual customers—th e customers we would expect to see at
food banks? No, they are not. Food banks are now facing a huge increase in the number
of people we would call the working poor—those who are in jobs but who cannot afford
to pay their bills. They cannot afford to pay a bill that comes out of the ordinary at the
time they have to pay it. They have jobs; they have jobs that are low-income jobs, and
many of them have two jobs, but they are amazed they have a Government that thinks
giving $15 an hour to those on the lowest income would be a bad thing for this country.
The Government talks about a loss of 6,000 jobs if we were to do that, but I have seen
no evidence that that would be the case. It is a made-up figure; it is made up because it
suits the Government to make it up and say it. But of course if the Government is going
to create 170,000 new jobs over the next 4 years,  then I suspect that if there were a loss
of 6,000 jobs, the Government would be able to find jobs somewhere else, would it not?
Of course, no one believes that 170,000 jobs will be created.
Then I went to Timaru and visited the food bank and the social service providers
there. The story they told me was very alarming. In Febr uary this year 157 people
received food parcels. By May the number had risen to 756—756. They have not seen
the like of the increase in working families receiving assistance. We are not talking just
of beneficiary families, but working families. This morning I went to the Newlands
Community Centre with Charles Chauvel. They told us they have seen a 300 to 400
percent increase in people going to their food bank, every year for the last 2 years. Does
that show us we have a country that is e qual? Does that show us we have a country
where people have an adequate income? No, it does not. The story these good people
told me this morning—they are not Labour  people; they are just good community
people—was of a woman who came in last week. She has a job and so does her
husband, but they are both on low incomes. Sh e came in for a food parcel, for the first
time in her life. Why? Because she had an abscessed tooth and she needed an extraction.
It cost $300 and she could not afford it. Finally, I went to Whangarei and there I heard
of the most appalling cases of health issu es and of a lack of food. There is growing
inequality in this country.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I want to talk about the Hon Phil
Goff. He is a nice man, Phil Goff. I quite like him. He has been an effective Minister in
his time, but his time is up. It is time for hi m to go. There are two reasons why I think it
is time that Phil Goff was out of here. The first reason is that that lot sitting over there
do not respect him. Watch their body language  when they are with him. They do not
respect him. In fact, they ar e so busy fighting one another th at he is left out on his own.
It was interesting to see when he appoint ed the new education spokesman, after the
Darren Hughes debacle. Whom did Goff appoint? He appointed his friend David
Shearer. He is a good friend. He brought him into Parliament. What did the Labour
caucus do? They rolled him, and they put in  Sue Moroney as the spokesperson on early
childhood education.
Sue Moroney spent 70 percent of the time at the estimates hearing last week talking
about early childhood educati on—the small part of pres chool. What about the big
compulsory sector? Where were the ques tions on that? Sue Moroney is so into
education she cannot even read  a Budget document. She belie ves that if there is a 5
percent increase in roll numbers, a 5 percent increase in the operations grant is needed.
It is no wonder the New Zealand Educational Institute loves her.
Speaking of which, the New Zealand Educational Institute sent out  postcards. It had
a postcard campaign: “Early Ch ildhood Education sets the scen e for life”. Turn it over
19600 General Debate 22 Jun 2011
and it says: “Dear Prime Minister”. This is a postcard to the Prime Minister. It says:
“Add your personal message to the Prime Minister and we will de liver it.” The post,
note here, is free: “ECE Campaign”. If you filled in this post card, who do you think
would get it? The New Zealand Educational Institute. And who would they give it to? It
would be the Prime Minister, because that is what it says.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It might be a valid
question, but I really do  not think that you would have filled in a postcard to be sent to
the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept the member’s point but I do not like interrupting speeches.
The member could have raised that point at the end of the speech.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Mr Speaker, I am sure you did not fill in a postcard. But if
you had filled in a postcard, would you not think that it would go to the Prime Minister?
Who do we think received these postcards? The Prime Minister? No. The Minister of
Education? No. The Minister of Finance, who controls the Budget? No.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who got them?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It was Sue Moroney. The New Zealand Educational Institute
ran a campaign, and who ended up with the campaign database? Sue Moroney. Poor old

items.speaker: Phil Goff said
items.text: “Actually, we were just going to write to these people to tell them what
was happening with the postcards.”
Our friend Whale Oil Beef Hooked has be en trawling through Labour emails for a
long time. The blogger from Whale Oil Beef Hooked has to be the email friend of the
world. He said he found an email sitting th ere, ready to go out from Sue Moroney,
which said things like “Last year, you filled in a postcard for the New Zealand
Educational Institute.” It talked about how Labour was fighting hard to stop the early
childhood education cuts: “Our focus will be quality … We need your support. …
Please like our Facebook page”, and share it with your friends. “Please feel welcome to
email me any time with your views. Kind re gards Sue Moroney”. Where is the Prime
Minister in all of this? Who has the postc ards? Does the Prime Minister have the
postcards? No. Sue Moroney has the postcards.
We know that Phil Goff does not know what is going on in his caucus; he has no
idea. Sue Moroney is working with the New Zealand Educational Institute, which is
supposed to be a union representing teac hers. Maybe Sue Moroney is mounting a
campaign with the New Zealand Educational In stitute for the leadership of Labour after
the next election. The New Zealand Educatio nal Institute has, by the way, launched on
its website a very active el ection campaign, so maybe Phil  Goff does not even know
what is happening to the election campaign. The New Zealand Educational Institute has
it all laid out, with a ll the targeted electorates for th e election campaign, and scripts for
conversations to have with people. It woul d be interesting to see whether Sue Moroney
is going out and talking to people in the context of early chil dhood education, saying
“Please think about signing our early chil dhood education petition here.”, and saying
things in the school context about children being able to learn at their own rate.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I seek leave to table two le tters from the office of the
Hon Phil Goff to the Prime Minister, John Key, asking him to accept the 20,000 New

items.text: Members cannot stand up and yell stuff out. If the Speaker has not

SU’A WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): We have a saying in Samoa: e maua
loa, kafiki loa, which means that when someone is caught doing something wrong, they
begin to attack. That is what we have hear d from the Minister of Education. If the
National leader had the cojones to accept t hose postcards, then they would not have
gone to Sue Moroney.
About this time in 2008 Mr John Key, the th en Leader of the O pposition, turned up
in my electorate flanked by two known Pacifi c former sports stars. There was a big
splash and a big ado about what they would do for the people of M āngere, the people of
Manukau, and the Pacific community. It was splashed in the paper that $6 million
would be invested in a trade academy at the Southern Cross Campus. Today that school
is still wondering where the rest of that money has gone. They are still wondering. The
two former sports stars who flanked the Prim e Minister at that time are nowhere to be
seen. They are not receiving answers to the questions about where that money has gone.
At that time, too, we told the community of M āngere that with National in
Government we would have to fight to prot ect ourselves; we woul d have to fight to
protect early childhood education; we would have to fight to protect housing, our public
health system, and our assets; and we woul d have to fight to protect the working
community of New Zealand. That is exactly what has transpired in the past 3 years
under a National Government. The first th ing it did was cut the budget for adult
community education, which served that co mmunity well. It continued to cut money
that went into early childhood education, which is significant for a population of
generally young people. Now we are hearing th at it will again be looking to undermine
the rights of workers not only through the 90-da y bill that it introduced right off the bat
but also by undermining the ability of trade unions and workers’ representatives to be
able to negotiate with employers.
With the high cost of living that we now have, prices are running up to 20 percent.
They are rising above more than what people  are earning. I ask this Government what it
will do for the working population the length and breadth of New Zealand when it has
given significant money to the wealthy few.  What will the Government do to enable
ordinary working families with children, who are struggling to make ends meet, to meet
the regular cost of living?
Let me give the House a couple of exampl es so that that side of the House
understands the struggles of working communities. There is a family in the south side of
Māngere who are currently living with tw o children in a Housing New Zealand
Corporation house. They have had to leave that house because it leaks and was not fixed
up by the Housing New Zealand Corporation. That family have to live with their parents
in a crammed-up situation. The promise that was given to the community of Māngere in
those days was that the Mi nister of Housing would fi x up the stock. Today many
fa
milies are still waiting for that housing stock to be fixed up.
A young man with a family of tw o children was sick in hospital in Ap ril. He had an
operation for cancer. He applied early, just prior to leaving hosp ital to go home, to
Work and Income New Zealand, and he was told  he was eligible for a sickness benefit.
19602 General Debate 22 Jun 2011
Today that family is still waiting to see whether they will receive a hand up to help them
with their normal day-to-day expenses, incl uding mortgage payments. They risk losing
their house because the culture of Governme nt departments under this Government has
changed significantly.
Labour recognises the hardship that fam ilies are working through. We promise the
working population of our comm unities and the rest of New Zealand that we will raise
the minimum wage to $15 an hour. Under this  Government we have had only a $1 rise
in the minimum wage after 3 years.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Like many
members in the House, I am always intrigued by what other political parties are up to. It
is fair to say that I have been looking on at the Labour Party in the last 12 months, and
the last 6 months in particular, to see exactly what its strategy is. It has been difficult for
me to untangle. Sometimes strategies ar e difficult to untangle because they are
complicated and clever, and one simply cannot see something coming. Sometimes
strategies are obvious to all and the team is proud of putting them forward and out there.
It has been difficult with the Labour Party. I must say that in recent times I have
actually identified a pattern. There is definite ly a pattern when it comes to the Labour
Party’s strategy. That pattern is about carving out Labour’s core support. It is essentially
setting aside those people w ho will not vote for Labour an d targeting those who will
vote for it.
Labour made a conscious decision. We know wh at it is. Labour said it did not want
the hobbit vote. Clearly, Labour does not want hobbits to vote for it. Labour does not
want the New Zealand film industry to vote for it. Labour does not think it is important
to bring that sort of income into New Zealand. Labour does not want the hobbit vote.
Labour does not support John Key making t hose advances to in ternational film
organisations to ensure that the  Hobbit  movies are filmed here. Labour opposed that.
Labour is against hobbits. That was one sector that the Labour Party decided it did not
want supporting it.
Labour then moved to the agriculture and farming sector, where we saw a tirade from
members over there saying that farmers do not  pay tax, they do not contribute to the
economy, they are essentially avoiding tax, and the Labour Party does not support them.
Furthermore, to really kick it to farm ers, the Labour Party decided to bring the
emissions trading scheme forward, put unknown costs on farmers, and make sure that as
soon as Labour is in Government after the next election—and that is Labour’s dream—
it will bring farmers into the emissions trading scheme. Labour has set aside the farmers
of New Zealand, and the farmers say that Labour is making agriculture the whipping
boy. Federated Farmers said of Stuarts Nash ’s tirade about farmers not paying tax and
the emissions trading scheme: “It’s all designed to discredit the farmers of New
Zealand.” There is a strategy.
Labour does not want the farmers to vote for it, it does not want th e hobbits to vote
for it, and, interestingly enough, it  has decided to insult the R ātana Church. An article
titled “Labour list insults Ratana Church” sa id: “Senior Ratana minister Kereama Pene
has launched a stinging Facebook campaign against what he sees as Labour’s list insult.

items.speaker: He said on the social networking site
items.text: ‘Every Ratana should show their total disgust and
abandon Labour forever.’ ” Labour has decided,  in carving out its core support, that it
does not want farmers, it does not want hobbits, and it does not want the Rātana Church.
Labour does not want homeowners; it is goi ng to introduce a capital gains tax. The
minute it is in Government, it will introdu ce a capital gains tax for all homeowners.
Labour does not want homeowners at all.
It was not enough to decide th at it wanted to carve off sector interest groups, so
Labour decided to go regional. It said to Northlanders that the highway from  Auckland
22 Jun 2011 General Debate 19603
to Northland is a “Holiday Highway” and that Labour would can it. Labour does not
want trucks, cars, and buses going to Northland, and it cer tainly does not want those
Northlanders coming south to Auckland. La bour has decided it does not want the
Northland vote, so it went regional.
As if regional was not enough, Labour decided to go international. On the eve of and
during the royal wedding, which we all enjoyed—not only New Zealanders but the
whole world—Phil Goff suggested that dr opping the monarchy should be up for
discussion. This happened during the royal wedding, which we  all celebrated. Phil Goff
decided that Labour had already set aside and isolated sectors and regions, particularly
Northland, so he went international. Do  members know who Phil Goff is? He is the
little guy at the back of the church who stands up and puts up his hand when the priest
asks whether anyone objects to this couple getting married. That is who Phil Goff is. He
is the little guy who puts up his hand and obj ects when the pastor asks whether those
royals should get married. What is Phil Goff doing?

items.speaker: Hon JIM ANDERTON
items.text: I do not participate very often in
these general debates, and in just the last couple of minut es I remembered why. What a
waste of space that speech by Phil Heatley was.
Yesterday in question time I asked the A ssociate Minister of Health Peter Dunne
what he had to say about the fact that nearly 3,000 young New Zealanders under 5 years
of age are admitted to public hospitals to  have their teeth removed under general
anaesthetic. He said he was very pleased w ith the fact that they had access to public
hospitals to have that done. It really stunned me that an Asso ciate Minister of Health in
charge of dental policy would be pleased by that. It almost blew my mind away. He
should be deeply concerned about the fact that 3,000 children are going to hospital to
have their teeth removed. They are the lucky ones, I tell members, because the others
who cannot get in are on waiting lists of be tween 6 to 12 months. Dr Beaglehole knows
a bit about this. He is the senior dental surgeon at th e Nelson Marlborough District
Health Board. He says that on Tuesdays a nd Fridays he spends mornings knocking out
children with a general anaesthetic so he can fix their rotting teeth. The toddlers and
preschoolers are so young they are too littl e to hold open their mouths long enough to
have it done in the regular way, and their ba by teeth are so decayed that nothing but
filling or extraction can save them. This is th e procedure that Peter Dunne is pleased is
available to these kids.
We should be asking ourselves what is doing all this. Well, members should ask
themselves this question: what is the most popular and most sold item in the
supermarkets of New Zealand? The answer is  a 2½ litre bottle of Coca-Cola. What is
the second most popular item in the supermarkets of New Zealand? It is a 1½ litre bottle
of Coca-Cola. If one goes in to the supermarkets now, one  sees that they have a
promotion for the drinks that make All Blacks—these Powerade drinks. There are 16
teaspoons of sugar in every single bottle. The ki ds are told to drink it as quickly as they
can, then they will become All Blacks. No, th ey will not; by age 10 to  18 they will join
the 500 type 2 diabetes sufferers that we have at the moment who are between the ages
of 10 and 18. As we speak, we have about 350,000 overweight New Zealanders who are
type 2 diabetes sufferers. We ha ve another 90,000—roughly a third—who are
undiagnosed, and we have an epidemic of dental decay that is  coming on us like a
tsunami because all of the people who are at  retirement age now who kept their teeth,
when years ago parents used to have their children’s teeth taken out for their birthday at
age 15 or 16, have to have their teeth looked after. We are making no provision for that.
Today I launched a dental policy to try to do something about it. In the few minutes I
have here I cannot detail it all, but I will say just one or two things. I looked at the
Australian situation with regard to, for ex ample, fluoride, which in water supply gives
19604 General Debate 22 Jun 2011
over 32 percent more protection to children’s teeth than no t having fluoride. If one
thinks about what that does in terms of th e kinds of operations th at Dr Beaglehole is
doing, one would be inclined to think that it should be a matter for public debate. Eighty
percent of all Australians have access to fl uoridated water. Even  the Queensland state
Government, which I have never thought of as being overly enlightened, had a meeting
in Parliament a year ago where the overwhel ming majority voted in favour of extending
fluoridation from 54 percent of the state to th e whole state. They voted for it practically
unanimously. They join the states of New South Wales, which supplies fluoridated
water to 92 percent of the stat e; South Australia, which su pplies fluoridated water to 94
percent of the state; and Vi ctoria, which supplies fluorid ated water to, I think, 80
percent of the state.
Here, fluoridated water is supplied to 60 percent of the whole of New Zealand. In the
mainland of the South Island, we have very little fluoridation. So the teeth of the
children of the most affluent families in Merivale and so on are much worse than those
of the children in South Auckland, where they have access to fluoridated water. Are we
proud of all this? Do we think something s hould be done about it? We should have a
national policy on fluoridation. We should have it as a national health measure, not at a
local body level where it is far too easy for local body politicians to hide. In
Christchurch recently we had chlorine a dded to our water, which was quite proper
because if we had not then we might be suffe ring from all kinds of endemic diseases as
we speak.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: What now?

items.speaker: Hon JIM ANDERTON
items.text: Chlorine—to clean up the water and make sure it is
drinkable. Yet if we suggest  adding fluoride, which cannot be smelt, seen, or tasted,
there is an uproar. I wonder at the double standards of that.
My Labour colleagues have been good enough to accept this policy as something
they will look at seriously for their health policy in the coming election. because I am
retiring at the end of this year. I am glad they are doing it and I wish them well.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I do not know what the Hon Jim
Anderton was talking about, but I can tell from even this distance that that member
needs to brush his teeth.
We in this party, unlike the party on the ot her side, are focused on the things that
matter: on the economy, on educational standards, and on doing something about crime,
which Labour has ignored. What is Labour fo cused on? Let us look at what Labour is
focused on. It is focused on voluntary student membership, or “VSM”. It is absolutely
focused on voluntary student membership. Labour members are filibustering—that is
not a world I like—other members’ bills—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Just wait and see.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: —sorry, I can hear something—s o that we do not get to the
voluntary student membership bill. I can tell members that the people of Tauranga, the
people of Rotorua, and the people of West Coast - Tasman do not even know what
“VSM” is.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: No, they’ll tell them to go to the doctor.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: That is right. Some of them think it is a contagious disease they
could get from members on the other side of the House. They do not  know what it is,
but, somehow, that is where all the energy on the other side of th e House goes. Why is
Labour putting all of its efforts into that bill? If we were generous, we could ask
whether it is doing it on prin ciple. Well, no, because the prin ciples at stake in that bill
are freedom and choice, which are actually Na tional Party values. That is why we are
putting that bill ahead.
22 Jun 2011 General Debate 19605
I have concluded that Labour’s reason is pu rely and solely politics. We know on this
side of the House that it does not take much thinking to see that for members opposite
their main training ground—some would sa y their only training ground—is in the
universities. Student politics is base camp, training cam p, for Labour Part y politicians.
We could go through them. Grant Robertson is  probably the main one  we can think of.
In his time he was the student union pr esident of one Michael Woodhouse. Student
politics is a Labour Party training ground.
Labour members do not want to stand up for freedom and choice; they are
filibustering on that bill purely because of politics. If I have  learnt anything in 2½ years
in this House, it is that the Labour Party only ever focuses on politics. In fact, that was
“Helen Clark 101”—politics is all. Everything is  about the politics, and we see it in that
bill.
We also know that the member opposite Trevor Mallard is interested in sports. He is
in a cycling competition. I understand that in his spare time he is also meant to be
campaign manager for the Labour Party, but why worry about that when he has a sports
competition to worry about. As one Cameron Slater has said: “Duck really needs some
anger management courses so he can concen trate on the campaign rather than fighting
an asymmetrical war with a right-wing blogger he can’t win.” Yet that is where the

items.speaker: Labour Party is at the moment
items.text: voluntary stud ent membership bills that people do not
understand, cycling races that are asymmetrical and they cannot win, and political
stunts. I think John Carter called them cunning stunts, and that  is what we are seeing on
the other side of the House.
With the State-owned enterprises referendum legislation we have already established
that because of Labour’s fili bustering, that bill has absolutely no chance of coming
before this House. As John Armstrong said in, I think, yesterday’s newspaper, Labour’s
member’s bill has about much chance of becoming law as that famous rugby-playing
country Namibia has of lifti ng the Rugby World Cup, or probably even less. But unlike
the New Zealand Labour Party, Namibia’s La bour Party has at least some chance—and
members can check this on the internet—of winning the next general election in that
country.
Why is it that Labour is putting forward the cheap politics of that  bill? Why is that?
If we look at the Prime Minister , he has never sold a State a sset, but if we put him head
to head with the leader of the Labour Party, he  has the best track record in this House of
selling State assets in this country.

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: How many has he sold?

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It is a pretty solid record. In  his career he has sold 17 State
assets, worth $9.49 billion.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Who did that?

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: That $9.49 billion worth of assets was sold by one Phil Goff.
Maybe we should go through them. There was New Zealand Steel, Petrocorp, Health
Computing Services, Development Finance Co rporation, the Post Office, the Shipping
Corporation, Air New Zealand, Land Co rporation, Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation, and Government Printing—the list goes on.
Debate interrupted.
