items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I think the message is clear this afternoon. If
anyone wants to witness how out  of touch this Government is, they need merely watch
the general debate on a Wednesday. When people tune in they will not hear a discussion
about the $16 billion deficit. They will not hear the Government’s plan to deal with
rising unemployment. They will not hear any discussion about inequality levels or the
increasing cost of living. No, instead, they will hear Anne Tolley make jokes about
postcards, they will hear Ph il Heatley try to make joke s about hobbits, and then they
will hear backbench open mike night via Simon Bridges. I have no idea what that was. I
am sure the people who were watching, unfortunately, had no idea what that was.
I think there is a much bigger issue. I do not want to allow myself to be distracted by
Mr Bridges’ speech. Instead, I would rather come  back to the point that this week in the
House we had an acknowledgment from the Minister of Labour that living on the
minimum wage in this country is very, very difficult. In fact, she talked about the tight
budget that many of those living on the mini mum wage are experiencing. I would say,
though, that the use of the term “tight budget” almost implies that there is some choice
for householders, whereas the Hon Annette King talked about the stark choices people
are making: fix a broken tooth or eat. T hose are kinds of choices that Kiwis are
currently making. That is not just a tight budget.
Living on the minimum wage has now become a lot harder under this Government.
Not only are we seeing an increase in prices of almost 5 percent; we are seeing increases
in ACC and in rent per week of almost 32 percent over the past 3 years.
For university students the cost of studying has increased by 16 percent. We see the
impact of that on young people. Student hard ship grants have increased by 423 percent
over the past few years, and much of that increase is due to an increase in the cost of
food for those students who are struggling to survive. So I ask the Minister of Labour
this question: if she acknow ledges that living on the mini mum wage is hard, how hard
will it be for a young person to live on a yout h minimum wage? How hard will it be for
a young person to live on less than what all Kiwis on the minimum wage are currently
surviving on? The Government has acknowledged  that it is considering the option of a
youth minimum wage. This is a pparently part of the Government’s cogent plan on jobs.
I think it probably speaks more to the point  that everything the Government has done
thus far has not had the impact required to  bring down record high levels of youth
unemployment—now 27 percent.
Labour says that paying young people less is not the answer. In re sponse we say that
is a cop-out. It is an acknowledgment that  the Government does not have the answers
and does not have a plan to create jobs. The G overnment thinks its only option is to try
to pay young people less in order to switch round the unemployment issue.
The Minister has openly stated that if  we pay young people less, then employers
might be more inclined to employ young peopl e instead of, say, 30-year-olds, but that
acknowledgment would potentially shift the unemployment issue from one age group to
22 Jun 2011 General Debate 19607
another. How does that overall  help New Zealand and Kiwi s who are out of jobs and
looking for work? It does not. I would be happy for any Government member to explain
to me how youth wage rates bring down une mployment across the board. I would be
happy to hear any evidence whatsoever.
I have some evidence I would like to present to the Government. It is the cold hard
fact that the lowest levels of youth unempl oyment were achieved under the last Labour
Government, and it was after youth wage rate s were abolished. Youth wage rates have
absolutely nothing to do with youth unemploym ent. In fact, we have evidence from the
Department of Labour that suggests there is no robust correlati on between youth wage
rates and youth unemployment. In fact, the 1990s, as members will well remember
when National was last in Government, wa s the last time that youth unemployment was
as high as it is now. We had youth wage rate s. It is time the Government acknowledged
that it is out of ideas, and that this measure will not help young people.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: That last speech by Jacinda Ardern has
shown us what is wrong with the Labour Opposition. It shows economic illiteracy: a
borrow-and-spend mentality, taking other people’s money and sharing it around, and
then telling New Zealanders th ey should be grateful and su pport Labour so it can keep
doing it. In my speech I will show a few contrasts.
On the one hand we have a Government that has worked hard over 2½ years to focus
on education so our children can get more and so their mothers and fathers can be
assured they will have a better future. We have a Government that has taken the hard
edges off the recession, that has focused on j obs, and that has been delivering for New
Zealanders. We have a Government that is particularly looking at what more it needs to
do with that forgotten generation of young people, who the last Government, over 9
years, thought could be made dependent and given welfare, and that that was OK. We
have made New Zealanders safer in the streets and in their homes through a raft of
legislation around law and order. On behalf of my constituen ts, I thank the Minister of
Justice and the Minister of Police for the hard work they have done over 2½ years to
make New Zealand a safer country, and to make sure that those who commit crimes and
who harm people in our communities are held to account.
The Minister of Finance, Bill English, has delivered a Budget that will get the New
Zealand economy back on track. Labour memb ers say they want to borrow more and
more and more, and they tell New Zealanders  that that is OK and not to worry about
that. Well, New Zealanders know that that is not something that is good for them, and is
not something that is possible. Bill English has delivered a Budget for us that will bring
New Zealand back to surplus much sooner—2013 or 2014. The other thing that we have
done is to get more from the Public Servic e. What that means for New Zealanders is
that for every dollar of income tax they cont ribute, their Public Se rvice is delivering
more for them in terms of hospitals, schools, and public services across the board.
On the other side of the House what do we hear? We hear about Labour’s shonky
economic policies and proposals. When Anne Tolley spoke earlier in this debate she
was right: there is a huge amount of confusion amongst members opposite, and, sadly,
most of that rests with the Leader of the Opposition, Phil Goff. Now, to his credit, when
he became the Leader of the Opposition, soon af ter the last election, I think that Labour
was right to have high hopes for him as L eader of the Opposition. Well, today standing
here when we consider its high hopes for the Leader of the Opposition, Phil Goff, we
see that the hope has gone. When one considers his economic policies, he might well be
high from time to time, because they ar e crazy and they are disastrous for New
Zealanders. Let us have a little look at th is. What have we heard over the last few
months of this year? We have heard lots of promises to spend, lots of policies that say
Labour will do more for New Zealanders. But when Mr Goff is asked where the money
19608 General Debate 22 Jun 2011
will come from, he has no answer. From memory, it would be $12 billion or $13 billion
of extra spending. We heard that he might scrap something in the area of defence, which
is a one-off spend, but that $13 billion of a dditional recurrent spending, year upon year
upon year, would have to be borrowed. New Z ealanders see through that façade. They
know it is not good for them, and they are aw ake to some of the false promises the
Opposition is making to them.
I think I know what the problem could be. I have just worked it out. When Mr Goff
first came to this Parliament I think I was 13 years of age. Simon Bridges was probably
7 years of age, and I guess the current memb er for Rimutaka, who will be the member
for Rimutaka for probably only about 4 more  months, was concei ved about then. So
what has happened in that intervening peri od? The last speaker from our side, Mr
Bridges from Tauranga, talked about asset sales. There was a wonderful column in the
newspaper just today from John Armstrong, a very astute  writer in the New Zealand

items.speaker: Herald
items.text: “Labour push against asset sales doomed to fail”. We have not heard a lot about
that this week, but it is doomed to fail—a very  astute reporter, that one. So what did
Phil Goff do when he was in Government? Se venteen State-owned assets were sold—
17 of them were sold. He sold more State-owned assets than any member of this House,
to my knowledge. I say to New Zealanders  listening, those who may hear of this
afterwards, do not trust that Opposition.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I did not want to interrupt the member’s speech. I ask you to reflect on whether
his speech was a reflection on you, as a more senior member than Mr Goff, as to being
around here too long.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We are not going to carry on this nonsense. That was not a point of
order.

items.speaker: RAHUI KATENE
items.text: There is a saying that until
recently I would not have been confident using, and that is the phrase “It ain’t over until
the fat lady sings”. But just as I am pr oud of my transformation, I am proud also to
stand today to speak of the tr ansformation that is occurring in Te Tai Tokerau as we cut
down to the wire.
When the M āori Party re-entered Te Tai Tokerau over the last few months to listen,
to learn, and to find out what the electorate needed, they told us they wanted someone
who would focus on being their voice. Th ey wanted someone who could build
relationships, who would be proactive and pos itive. They wanted a representative who
could make a constructive contribution. They wanted IWI: influence with integrity.
Few areas of New Zealand so desperately need that influence to be acted on as Te
Tai Tokerau. The statistics scream out for such a focus: 49 percent of children were
identified as being born in the most deprived  areas. In 2010 the Northland rate for acute
rheumatic fever was nearly three times the national rate. In fact, a study in Kaitāia found
that one child in every 100 had evidence of heart damage caused by rheumatic fever. In
some of the poorest areas of the region 40 pe rcent of children were living in crowded
households. In the past year more than 7,000 Northlanders have been given food parcels
by social services. No member of Parliament , no matter what their affiliation, can listen
to these statistics without being moved. But we  must do more than simply talk about it
and hope the problems will go away.
The M āori Party has taken this analysis very  seriously. We have taken immediate
and comprehensive action to address both the long-term nature of poverty and the
specific priorities for education, health, and social services in the region. Last December
I wrote to every m
ember of this House asking for their support in addressing child
poverty. Today at the Māori Affairs Committee the Aotearoa Equality Group tabled our
22 Jun 2011 General Debate 19609
request for an inquiry to place on record our united concern for the pervasive disparities
and poor outcomes being experienced by Māori children.
Just over a month ago my colleague Tari ana Turia announced that the Government
would prioritise $12 million of investment into addressing and preventing rheumatic
fever—an announcement that Ng āpuhi general practitioner Dr Lance O’Sullivan hailed
as worthy of our greatest support.
We have also worked to wrap support around wh ānau though the enormous
investment made through Wh ānau Ora. Three incredible collectives of M āori providers
have been revitalised through Wh ānau Ora to support whā nau across their region. The
Te Tai Tokerau Wh ānau Ora collective includes Whakawhiti Ora Pai, Te Hauora o Te
Hiku o Te Ika, Te R ūnanga o Te Rarawa, Ng āti Hine Health Tr ust, and Kia Ora Ng āti
Wai. Another seven providers are brought together in Te Hau Āwhiowhio o Ō tāngarei,
and another seven in Te Pū o te Wheke.
The Minister of M āori Affairs has supported Wh ānau Ora with complementary
initiatives such as Ōranga Wh ānau. By virtue of the Kaitoko Wh ānau programme in
Kaitāia, Te Korowai Aroha trust has helped 53 whānau access social assistance services.
Also approximately 75 r ōpū in the region have accessed the M āra Kai gardening
programme to equip and establish gardens at marae, at kura, at k ōhanga, and,
importantly, at home.
Te Tai Tokerau homes have benefited directly from the 6,000 homes insulated as a
result of the M āori Party negotiating a 100 percen t subsidy for housing insulation for
those with community services cards. Some 638 rangatahi in Northland and another 247
rangatahi in Auckland have benefited fr om Community Max positions, which provide
an entry point into longer-term employment options. We are particularly proud of the
heavy investment we have made in education, with support for literacy programmes and
more funding for kura kaupapa Māori, for transport to school, and for programmes such
as Te Kotahitanga that support M āori success in education. Over $100 million was
earmarked for Māori education in the Budget and $73 million for kura kaupapa.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I was fascinated by a tête-à-tête that took
place a couple of weeks ago between Mr Ma llard and Heather Roy over the costs of
running our democracy, in response to Mrs Roy’s criticism of Labour’s outrageous
filibustering on m
embers’ day. She estimat ed that that nonsense was costing the
taxpayer about $453,000 per hour. Mr Mallard replied that silly Heather Roy could not
do the maths, and that her maths was predi cated on the assumption that Parliament had
sat longer than it would have otherwise. He sa id she needed to brief her intern on the
difference between average and marginal costs.
Well, I am a chartered accountant, so I know a bit about marginal costs. If one picks
up a textbook, one finds it will say something a bout the costs attributable to the next
unit of production. Here is the problem: on members’ day nothing is being produced—
absolutely nothing. So Heather Roy’s maths was absolutely accurate, and half a million
dollars per hour is being wast ed, every single hour. The cost of the Te Tai Tokerau by-
election, which the Labour Party heavily criticised, is being wasted by its members
every single hour of members’  day. It is like that Yes, Minister episode. Remember the
empty hospital? It had all the staff, the ad ministrators, and the doctors, but it did not
have any patients. Well, this Parliament every second Wednesday has the members, the
security guards, the clerks, and the Hansard staff, but we  are not producing a single
thing.
We have also heard about the total stunt th at Phil Goff’s member’s bill on asset sales
is. Mr Bridges has already quoted the excellent article by John Armstrong about
Namibia having more chance of winning the Rugby World Cup than that bill has of
being enacted. But John Armstrong also said that even if Labour became the
19610 General Debate 22 Jun 2011
Government, that bill could not  pass. It is framed up as entrenching legislation, which
requires 75 percent of the House’s support, so the Labour members know that it cannot
pass even if they become the G overnment. It is a stunt. It would be silly if it were not
for the fact that members’ day is a very im portant part of our parliamentary process,
where those outside the executive get to debate and raise the legislation and bills that
are important to them and their constituents. I thought that Labour’s backbenchers
would be pretty annoyed at th e way in which that was going, except that we have not
had a member’s bill ballot this year. I went  back to November 2010, the last ballot that
we had. There were 25 bills in that ba llot. Do members know how many there were
from Labour?

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: None.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: One. There was one bill from a Labour member in the
last member’s bill ballot that we had. Do  members know whose bill that was? It was
Darren Hughes’ bill on transport, so who know s where that is? Labo ur is so keen to
represent its constituency that its members cannot come up with a single bill, except one
that is a stunt. They know it is a stunt. Th at is how half a milli on dollars an hour is
being wasted on every single members’ day.
What are the Labour members doing if they  are not actively participating in our
democracy? Well, they are alienating themselves  from just about every sector. We have
certainly heard about the farmers. I did not think that the Labour members would go and
slap the Rātana Church, which has been very loyal to Labour for a long time. The public
tell me that they are sick and tired of th e same old rhetoric: “There is no plan.”, and
“Where are the jobs?”. The public know; they  are getting to it. They understand how
hard things are, and they understand that this Government does have a plan.
The Government’s plan involves a provi ding a taxation system that works and
rewards effort. The plan is al so about having an education an d skills training plan. It is
about fostering free trade and innovation in  science. It is about investing in
infrastructure, and billions of dollars are going into infrastructure, not the least of which
is in the South Island and in Canterbury. It includes putting a lid on Government
spending. This Government makes no apologie s for the fact that there are opportunities
to continue to constrain spending and for expecting a lot more to come out from a little
more going in. And the Gove rnment’s plan is about reducing compliance costs to
business. One does not need to be a mathematician to work out that if nominal GDP
growth of 8 percent is achieved, that will produce a minimum of 200,000 jobs in this
economy. Those members ask where the jobs will come from. Well, it is pretty obvious:
they will come from a growing economy. Th ey will not come from bureaucrats and the
public sector. We might have to increase the number of jobs by 172,000 in order to
offset the very small reduction in public se ctor workers that has taken place. I am
extremely pleased to put those plans and policies up against Labou r’s any day of the
week.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: What a relief to hear at least one member on the
other side of the House talk about his own party for a change, instead of spending the
entire 5 minutes talking about the Labour Party. I am very, ve ry interested, actually; it
makes me wonder why those members are so  concerned about the Labour Party. Why
do they want to talk about us all the tim e? I know that Mr Woodhouse will not like me
saying this, but I think it demonstrates th at those members have nothing good to say
about themselves, and no plan for the future. Labour will give everybody a fair go and
make everybody pay their fair share. I am very proud to say that Labour has a solid
promise to raise the minimum wage to $15 by the end of its first year in Government.
That is a solid promise. So do not say that we do not have policies. We will do better by
low and middle income people who are struggling to make ends meet.
22 Jun 2011 General Debate 19611
Let me talk about what an increase in the minimum wage to $15 an hour will mean.
It will mean that over 229,000 workers will get a lift in their pay, if they work full-time,
of almost $80 a week. Labour’s tax-free threshold adds a further $10 a week. The
people who will benefit from this are not  just young workers; they are women, Mā ori,
Pasifika, and those up in Northland, in Te Tai Tokerau, who are struggling to make ends
meet. There would be an economy-wide incr ease in wages of $518 million. That is an
economic plan.
We all know that National’s changes have not helped anybody. They have not helped
unemployment, they have not helped wages, and they have not helped those on the
lowest wages, as the Minister of Labour adm itted today and yesterday. But, of course,
that Minister of Labour did not  want the minimum wage to go up from $12 an hour last
year. She actually rejected the proposition th at it should go up at all, but was rolled.
Then she wanted to keep it at $12 an hour. This year the advice was that the minimum
wage could go up to $13.50 with a negligible impact on jobs. Sh e rejected that as well;
she ignored that advice. John Key’s Govern ment is making life tougher for working
people when things were already hard. National did it the last time it was in
Government, and New Zealand went backwards in wages, productivity, skills
development, and job creation. Now it is at it again.
But New Zealanders are not stupid. They are moving across the Tasman in droves—
in greater numbers than ever before—becau se they have worked out that this
Government has no answers. People are not stupid. They can see that Australia has a
minimum wage of NZ$20 an hour, and that differential is a problem for this
Government and this country. Those worker s getting on the planes are not just the
highly skilled; they are also  the unskilled, because they can do better across the Ditch.
Those workers cannot make a living in this  country, because this Government is
miserable with the minimum wage and has no plan to provide them with decent jobs.
Contrary to popular opinion, more than half of all workers covered by the minimum
wage are older than 24. So it is not just about young workers trying to get into work. It
affects good people. It affects our school suppor t staff. It affects our caregivers—those
who look after older people—our home-care workers, and our hospital and school
service staff, among thousands and thousands. Let us talk about what a minimum wage
earner actually takes home each week. If they work full-time—and many of them do
not—they earn $447 a week after tax. That is before reductions for KiwiSaver, student
loans, if they have one, or ACC. John Key’s cleaner in this Parliament is paid $13.10 an
hour. I bet that no one, particularly the Minister of Labour, asked her advice about
whether increasing the minimum wage beyond $13 was a good idea. I do not understand
how anyone expects people to live on $447 a w eek. That is what a full-time worker gets
on the minimum wage. I do happen to know that Kate Wilkinson has not been anywhere
near her cleaners or the Prime Minister’s cl eaners, because if she bothered to talk to
them she would know that her decisions are making life even tougher.

items.speaker: Hon Dr WAYNE MAPP
items.text: We have certainly heard Labour’s
plan now. It will put an extra $500 million of costs on employers into the economy—
$500 million extra costs on employers. What woul d that do? It is quite simple, really.
Essentially, it would reduce the productive capacity of the ec onomy. This is the choice
New Zealand is really faced with at the moment: the economic plan. We heard one part
of Labour’s economic plan: add costs into the economy. Labour members actually think
that that is a plan. They think a sympathy a pproach to the economy w ill do it. I have to
say that that is simply a cynical and bankrupt attempt to grow the economy.
This is what Labour’s plan seemingly is. First of all, Labour would increase the
minimum wage, which would mean $500 million extra against employers. Second,
Labour would increase borrowing. Third, Labour would increase departm
ental
19612 General Debate 22 Jun 2011
expenditure. Just about every spokesperson across the House has made some promise or
other to increase departmental expenditure. La bour is against efficiency. It is against
broadband, even. It will have the opportunity later today, no doubt, to decide whether to
vote for that infrastructure investment or against it. I apprehend, based on the debate
that I have heard so far, that Labour will vote against it. It is against broadband, it is
against infrastructure, and it is against irri gation. It consistently  opposes the plans to
expand irrigation in the Canterbury region.
What other things is Labour against? It is against the sale of State-owned enterprises.
Yesterday, when I was listening to the de bate, Labour’s core argument was that New
Zealanders already own those a ssets. That is a complete mi sunderstanding of what it is
about. We could have said that about a Po lish shipyard. The people already owned the
Polish shipyard. What did the Polish people do? They decided, in common with every
Eastern European citizen, that their already owning it was not the way to prosperity. In
fact, the way to prosperity was to actually have a personal share in that business. Our
mixed-ownership model will build the capacity  of the New Zealand Exchange and give
New Zealanders, including KiwiSaver account hol ders, the opportunity to directly own,
and to have a personal stake in, the economy of New Zealand. They will personally see
the gains. It is well known—and Labour shoul d know this; at least Mr Mallard knows
this—that having some private sector owne rship increases efficiency and increases
effectiveness. Of course, it enables the Government to invest against borrowing.
We have already heard about what Labour sold when it was in office in 1989. Would
Labour members seriously suggest today that New Zealand taxpayers should own
Telecom? Would they seriously suggest toda y that it would be a good idea to have a
network of State hotels? Would they seriously suggest today that we should have a rural
bank finance banking system? Would they seriously suggest today that it would be a
really good idea for the Government to own New Zealand Steel? That is the space they
are in now. They are now in the space of sayi ng that anything that is publicly owned
must always remain in public ownership, 100 percent. The reason for that is that we
already own it. To Labour members, that is the complete answer. It is a mantra for them.
Yet from their own evidence, based on their record—including Mr Mallard—they know
that there are some situations where it is  better, frankly, to have private sector
ownership. Most of us would agree that th at balance already ex ists with Air New
Zealand, and we can see the advantages of that. That is why National is going to go out
to the public with that plan.
Another issue I want to raise is science a nd innovation. There was the big speech at
the Labour Party conference, where Sir Pa ul Callaghan, well known and well regarded
for his ideas on innovation, who wrote an excellent book called Wool to Weta , was
present. And what did Labour members do? They said they would bring back a $160
million tax credit. What will they fund that with? The bringing-in of the emissions
trading scheme 2 years earlier than planne d for farmers. That is a zero-sum game.
Labour has no plan.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
TELECOMMUNICATIONS (TSO, BROADBAND, AND OTHER MATTERS)
In Committee
Debate resumed from 21 June.
22 Jun 2011 Telecoms (TSO, Broadband & Other Matters) Amdt Bill 19613
Clauses 1 to 3

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I think it is fair to say that the
debate on the preliminary clauses is one in wh ich there is a certain review of what has
happened. In particular, we go to the appropria teness of the dates and times that are set
out. I think it is also fair to say that Labour will not be heavily opposing clause 3 of the
bill. It is probably the best clause in the whol e bill. It is one of the few that the Minister
for Communications and Information Tec hnology has managed to get right and get
through unamended. It is probably an indicatio n of the problems the Minister has had
with the bill that there are so few clauses within the bill that are unamended.
I think it is also fair to say that one coul d invent a number of mo re appropriate titles
for the bill. For example, we could call it the “Telecommunications (TSO, Broadband,
Telecom Subsidy, and Avoidan ce of Regulatory Matters) B ill” or a number of other
things.
It is probably important at this stage to restate Labour’s point of  view vis-à-vis the
bill overall and to restate the warnings that have  occurred earlier. I want at this stage to
thank Dr Brash. I am not quite sure of the rules and whether we ar e allowed to address
people outside the Chamber, but in passing I thank Dr Brash for drawing the attention
of the media to some comments I made last week during the Committee stage.
It is important to make clear that this legislation will be the subject of a review by the
new Government. The implication of that is that there will be more legislation that
drops out in 2020 and 2019 than there is curren tly. With that goes a warning that with a
change in the regulatory method and in th e financial arrangements, people who enter
into this sort of arrangement do so at some risk.
I have heard some criticism from memb ers opposite—though, notably, not from Sir
Roger Douglas. I thought it was telling that Sir Roger Douglas, who does actually
understand regulatory reform and the righ t of Governments to make changes going
forward, was not at all critical, whereas Dr Brash, who is opposed to broadband and
made it clear during his task force report th at he thought Government involvement in
broadband was a waste of money, was critical.
We have made it very clear that the Comm erce Commission will be involved in this
area in a way that it is not allowed to be under the current legislation. That could well
have—it will almost certainly have—implica tions in the regulatory arrangements for
Telecom, if, in fact, it positions itself to get into this contract. The difference between
this approach and, say, the approach used in the past by, for example, Sir Robert
Muldoon is that there is clear notice of this  fact before Telecom makes the decision to
structurally separate and before the final co ntractual arrangements become effective. So
if Telecom chooses to continue down this track, it will do so in the full knowledge that
there is a very real possibility of a change in regulatory environment within the term of
this arrangement and that it is at some risk of not being able to have what any thinking
person would regard as excessi ve profit and an excessive regulatory advantage during
that time.
It is nothing that could be compared to th e Chilean experience, for example, or that
of a number of other countries where there have been nationalisation-type approaches
without notice. It may be that for regula tory change and legislation change, the
legislation is reviewed and changed a nd the Commerce Commission is involved. Both
Telecom and Chorus are at some risk in th is, and both of them are satisfied with the
ongoing situation. But there is a ve ry real risk if this matter is not made clear to them. I
am sure that Steven Joyce, being a respons ible Minister and, in fact, one who would
probably like to stir the pot as well, will make  clear to Telecom the risks that sit there
for the company, including this particular ris k. There is probably a whole pile of other
19614 Telecoms (TSO, Broadband & Other Matters) Amdt Bill 22 Jun 2011
risks he is not prepared to tell Teleco m about, but I think it is becoming clear to
Telecom that it does not have legislative certainty over the period of this contract.
A point I want to make and really reinforce is that there is nothing this Government
can do by way of contractual arrangements th at indemnifies Telecom against future
legislation. It has to be made absolutely cl ear in this Chamber that no Parliament can
bind a future Parliament. This Parliament will not be and can never be in the position
whereby it is bound by a predecessor. Each Parliament is unique, and each has the
ability to make decisions. If a Parliament makes changes, it could well be criticised for
them and that might be appropriate, but that  is something we want to make clear will
not happen.
There are a number of things that one coul d do in order to defer this legislation
coming into force. Again, I acknowledge Sir Roger Douglas and the fact that he has
taken a principled position on this legislation.  I think it is relatively unusual to share
some of his views in relation to the quality of regulation. I find it very surprising that
Rodney Hide, the current Minister for Regul atory Reform, could possibly vote for such
an abuse of regulatory powers as forms part of  this bill. But it is good to know that at
least some of the ACT members are prepared to act by the party’s principles.
The party I very much have regret for in re lation to its position and its stated vote on
this legislation coming into force is the M āori Party, because through this legislation it
is undermining a significant Mā ori asset in 2degrees. There has been a lot of argument
over a period of time about the appropriatene ss of the decisions I was part of back in
2000, when working at the time with Bill Os borne, as I remember now—I do not know
whether Bill is even still involved—in order, if we like, to avoid—

items.speaker: Hon Rick Barker
items.text: Did you ever play football with him?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I did play football with Bi ll Osborne, and I lasted the
game and he did not. Poor old Bill ended up with a rather severe heart problem as a
result of that game. It was not a heart problem of the sort that Bill, in his playing days,
might have been more renowned for.
The point I am making is that  this change is one that significantly undermines the
assets of 2degrees. It means that that compa ny will be much less competitive and that it
will find it much harder to attract capital. I think it is bad that M āori are treating M āori
so badly.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is traditional in the debate at
the Committee stage on the title and commencement clauses to use the debate on the
title to draw together some of the themes  of the discussion. The Opposition is with a
certain sense of sadness, I guess, witnessing the Telecommunications (TSO, Broadband,
and Other Matters) Amendment Bill moving its way through the Committee. Maybe
one could call it the “What a Difference a Day Makes Bill”, if that day were the day of
the last election. There is a contrast betw een the regulatory framework that was pro-
competitive, which led to an upswing in investment and a better deal for consumers
under the previous Government, and this slid e back to the bad old days of Maurice
Williamson’s wet bus ticket, where the legi slation favoured the dominant incumbent.
Here, sadly, we are creating a new monopoly structure on fibr e to replace the existing
monopoly or dominant structure—or the pre-reform dominant structure—on copper.
There are a number of reasons why that is true. The first is the so-called regulatory
forbearance period—the regulatory holida y—that the Government proposed, which
took the cop off the beat. The Commerce Co mmission is the industry cop that stops
people from abusing market power, but that  regulatory holiday w ould have tied the
industry cop’s hands for a decade. That wa s obviously a nonsense. As my colleague
Trevor Mallard said, it is a matter of great regret that only late in the piece did the Māori
Party apparently wake up and have a discu ssion with the Government about that period,
22 Jun 2011 Telecoms (TSO, Broadband & Other Matters) Amdt Bill 19615
which apparently led to some change, alt hough not good change. Part of the regulatory
holiday is still there on point-to-multipoint  services, which in Labour’s view is
inappropriate, and which the Minister for Communications and Information Technology
has never explained.
More important, the rest of the regulatory forbearance period has been exchanged for
a taxpayer-funded guarantee to an incumbent. If it is caught out in future years with
excessive margins because the cost of providing the service has fallen but the price has
not, that incumbent will not pay if it is  penalised by the Co mmerce Commission; the
taxpayer will pay. That is extraordinary. An extraordinary insult is being added to
injury; the original injury wa s to the regulatory coherence of this industry. That is why
everybody in the industry, except for the in cumbent telecommunications company, was
united in saying that the Government’s legi slation was utter and absolute rubbish. The
Finance and Expenditure Committee heard submission after submission and, although
the submitters raised a range of issues, they were unanimous—other than Telecom—
that this bill should not proceed. But here we are. What a difference a day makes. The
Government is simply using its numbers to put through what in its heart of hearts it
must know—the Minister must know—is simply misguided legislation.
The second key issue why this is a very, very bad bill concerns the lack of rigour in
the open access regime. That is less important, we agree, in terms of retail, because we
assume that the structural separation of  Telecom will proceed, but it is crucially
important in wholesale and netw ork access. It is crucially impor tant in that critical dark
fibre access, where other wholesalers now have  no guarantee that they will be able to
access the same product, at the same price and in the same way, that Chorus will
provide to its own. We are re placing a problem of vertically integrated dominance on
copper with a new problem on fibre. That will mean that everybody who is in the
gallery watching will pay too much for their broadband in years to come—for at least a
decade to come—under this bill.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Or for their copper.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: That is right. Mr Mallard raises an important point—it is
the next one on my list—which is the manda tory averaging on copper pricing. The
broadband costs in fibre are so high that the only way the Government could make it
worthwhile for the industry to play was to raise the price on everybody’s existing phone
bill, for no change in service. The brief to us said that it would be $5 a month extra for
the average house in a city. But the price will now be averaged, as a matter of
Government policy, between city consumers and rural consumers. Once again, it looks
as if the farming sector is getting a sweet  deal out of this Government, while urban
consumers are being penalised.
I tell people that their phone bills are be ing put up by this Government to make it
look like a better deal—or a no-worse deal—for them to swap to fibre, which is too
expensive. Why is it too expensive? Becau se the Government subsidy was inadequate.
There was not enough money, but the Government  wanted a commercial rate of return
on the deal. The telecommunications company sa id it could not pay, so the Government
sold the law to the tune of what the o fficials have advised was between $400 million
and $600 million of disguised subsidies. It made the rules slacker and allowed the
telecommunications companies to rip off the consumer. That is an outrage; it sets the
course of the industry back a decade.
It was painful to get the progress that was made, but the progress was real—the
progress was real. Here is the proof of  the pudding: New Zealand climbed up the
broadband rankings in the “noughties”, but it has fallen back since 2008 from being
about 5th or 6th on those criteria to being about 12 th or 13th. We have tumbled down the
international rankings, because the Government and this Minister went around parading
19616 Telecoms (TSO, Broadband & Other Matters) Amdt Bill 22 Jun 2011
the $1.5 billion broadband plan, but—like ever ything else under this dishwater-shallow
National administration—there never was a plan.
There never was a plan. There was a marketing slogan, designed by Crosby/Textor or
some foreign spin doctor, to get National elected, but there never was a plan. I can think
of no other reason why it took an intelligent man like Steven Joyce 2½ years of nothing
to come up with a policy. But 2½ years later he has come up with an absolutely rotten,
retrograde policy that will set the industry back a decade. It will cost everybody in the
gallery, and everybody out in New Zealand, 5 bucks a month more on their existing
phone bills, and will consign them to higher prices on broadband—ultra-slow
broadband—for 10 years to come. This is not UFB—ultra-fast broadband. It is USB—
ultra-slow broadband. It took Steven Joyce ne arly 3 years to think up a set of dumb
rules that cost the public too much money: mandatory averaging, an open access regime
that does not work, and a stupid regulatory  holiday that even in the end the Mā ori Party
could not support.

items.speaker: Here is the next bit
items.text: an asset split. Th is Government is supposed to be running the
show. How do members like this? Telecom gets to decide how it structurally separates
and it tells the Minister only after the fact . After the board has signed off to its own
internal commercial satisfaction, the Minister has zero prerogative to override the
substance and zero requirement to consult the industry, and Telecom—how do members
like this—has zero requirement to put all the details in the public domain. A summary
of the asset split is OK. Who would know? If  I were running that company now, and
under an obligation to my shareholders to ma ximise profit, I could certainly hide a few
lurks and perks in the detail that neither the Minister no r the public would ever know
about until it was too late. Has the Government  been asleep for the last 20 years? Does
it not know the games that are pl ayed in this industry? Why is it playing back into the
hands of dominant incumbents and creati ng a new problem of monopoly on wholesale
fibre, just as existed with copper?
There is much more to say, but I will not go through it all now. This bill is so bad
that it probably breaches New Zealand’ s World Trade Organization undertakings,
because it is a disguised subsidy to a local  incumbent. How bad is that? It also
probably—or possibly, we should say; there is conflictin g advice on this—conveys
some favourable tax treatment on certain members of the industry. We are not quite sure
about that, but it certainly was not case proven in the select committee.
To sum up very briefly, this is the “What  a Difference a Day Makes Bill”. We used
to have fast broadband, but now we get ultra-slow broadband. People are paying too
much for their phones. They will be consigne d to slower, more expensive fibre than
they would have had if this bill was not passed.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I would like to focus my comments on the
commencement date and the interrela tionship between the clauses in the
Telecommunications (TSO, Broadband and Other Matters) Amendment Bill that were
to have limited the ability of the Commer ce Commission to intervene in the event of
uncompetitive practices by participants in the telecommunications industry and the
clauses that are said to be in the contr acts under which the Crown indemnifies Telecom
in respect of all losses it may have in the future if it is found to  have been acting anti-
competitively and loses some of its revenue th at it was otherwise expecting to get. How
could this be relevant? It is possible that, in  the future, part of Telecom could act in a
way that abuses its dominant position. There is no doubt that once Telecom builds this
fibre network, it will be the dominant supp lier of wholesale fibre in the country. If
Telecom abuses that and charges some of its competitors too much or some of its
consumers too much, then consumers lose from  both the loss of vitality of competition
from other telecommunication providers and facing higher prices than need be the case.
22 Jun 2011 Telecoms (TSO, Broadband & Other Matters) Amdt Bill 19617
We have already heard Davi d Cunliffe comment that one of the effects of the
Government’s policy in this area is to force up the price for people who do not have
broadband. The consequence of the arrangement s that the Government  has seen fit to
enter into with Telecom is that those who get their internet conn ections through the
copper network will be forced to pay a higher price than they would pay if nothing had
been done. One of the reasons for that is to have a lesser price difference between
internet services on copper networks and internet services on broadband fibre networks,
or fibre-based broadband networks, in an effort to improve for Telecom the likely take-
up of fibre-based broadband. The cost differential will not be as great, as the price of
copper has been pushed up falsel y. The effect of this bill is  just that. People who have
existing services will be paying more for th em. There will also be a cross-subsidy from
urban areas to rural areas.
This is part of a pattern that we see from this Government. The latest Budget
provided a subsidy of $35 million, I think, to the rural sector for new irrigation schemes.
At the very time when the Government will not support jobs in the KiwiRail workshops
to build wagons, it is subsidising the agricultur al sector to that tune . We also have this
cross-subsidy in respect of the telecomm unications industry, whereby copper wire -
based internet connections will be charged a falsely high amount in order to make the
gap between the price for that service and the price for fibre-based broadband smaller.
One can understand why the La bour Party is critical of th ese decisions. Indeed, we are
also critical of the f act that there was an over-promise , really, before the election, as
National said it would have the fast roll-out  of broadband. Here we are, 2½ years into
the National Government’s term, and it is onl y just passing the legislative framework.
The final contracts have not even been signed. The fibre that has to be physically put in
place to deliver broadband has not even started to be laid, pursuant to the Government’s
policy arrangements.
I am intrigued by how the provisions rela ting to Commerce Commission supervision
of this industry have metamorphosed over the period of this legislation’s stages. The bill
when introduced into the H ouse provided that there woul d be relief from Commerce
Commission supervision of this industry, a nd this was achieved by Part 2 inserting
some changes into the Commerce Act. This effectively ousted the jurisdiction of the
Commerce Commission to take action, even if it found that there was anti-competitive
practice on the part of a dominant participan t in the industry. That ran into problems.
There was severe criticism of that move at the Finance and Expenditure Committee by
other industry participants who thought that that was inappropriate. They foresaw the
risk that Telecom, if it was the successful contracting party with the Government, would
do in the future what Telecom has done in the past, which is to use its position of
dominance to the detriment of both consumers and other industry competitors. They
danced and jumped up and down and said th at this is wrong. They convinced every
political party in this House,  other than National, that th ey were right and National was
wrong.
As a consequence, National faced the reality  that it would not be able to pass the
legislation in this House in its then form . There were doubts from the ACT Party, from
the Māori Party, from the Greens, and from Labour —all of which said that we should
learn from our history. Overly  permissive regulatory regimes are taken advantage of by
dominant telecommunications company players,  to the detriment of consumers. If we
are creating a dominant player with monopoly powers, we ought to make sure that they
are overseen with proper regulat ory powers on the part of the regulator,  in this case the
Commerce Commission. In the face of the rea lity that the Government probably could
not have passed the legislation in that form , the Minister brought forward very late in
the process, through a Supplementary Order Paper to this Committee, changes that
19618 Telecoms (TSO, Broadband & Other Matters) Amdt Bill 22 Jun 2011
backed away from some of those cha nges to the Commerce Commission’s powers.
Again, we do not have the benefit of what the competitors in the industry might think of
that, because they have had no opportunity to submit on what is now proposed.
In return for the Government moving away  from removing those powers from the
Commerce Commission, we are to ld that instead it has conferred an indemnity under
the form of the contract that it proposes to enter into with Telecom. The indemnity
promises Telecom that if it loses revenue because of a future Commerce Commission
action, then the Government will make good that diminution in revenue even though the
abuse of its dominant position in the market would have been the basis for that revenue
being taken off Telecom in the first place. The Minister in the chair, the Minister for
Communications and Information Technology, is shaking his head and saying that that
is not the case, but, of course, the trouble we have with that is that we have not seen the
nature of these indemnity clauses. We are told  in the media that that is the effect of
these indemnity clauses—that the Governme nt will be indemnifying Telecom against
all losses occasioned by Comm erce Commission risk. That is  how I would paraphrase
it. If we have that wrong, well, how are we to know? At this stage when we are passing
this legislation, how are we to know? There is a lack of transparency in relation to what
exactly is proposed.
Labour will be voting against the commencement and title clauses of this—

items.speaker: Paul Quinn
items.text: David, that’s sad.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: It is sad, is it not? It is sad because we th ink there should
be regulatory certainty that goes beyond one Parliament. We do not think it  is desirable
that there is regulatory uncertainty. It is tr ue that that creates uncertainty for market
participants, not just for Telecom, which is the market participant in this context that the
Government keeps focussing on, but also for the other telecomm unications providers.
We need them to be secure in their future  business models in order to compete and to
cost-effectively provide services to New Z ealand consumers, so that we have real
competition in this market rather than being even more reliant on the dominant
provider, Telecom.
We have a number of problems with the pro cess that has been adopted to get here in
terms of the legislation, the delays we have had in the practical implementation of
broadband policy, and the bad policy we have as an outcome of those matters.
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): Perhaps I can provide some helpful a ssurances about a few things for Mr
Parker, in particular, although in answer to  his question about what we will do about
these things, I tell him that he could thi nk. Thinking would be a good thing, for starters.
One of the things he could think about would be the chances of a fibre network having a
monopoly position at any time in the next 8½ years. He could contemplate that, for a
kick-off. He could contemplate the fact that the copper network continues to be

sections.heading: New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill

items.text: In Committee
Part 1  Amendments to principal Act

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise to take a call on Part 1 of the New Zealand
Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill. Points have already been made in earlier
parts of the debate about how it was unfortu nate that submissions on the bill to the
22 Jun 2011 New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill 19623
Intelligence and Security Committee were heard in secret. I think the unnecessary
nature of that secrecy is emphasised by th e number of people who are in the gallery
today. The number of people present in the ga llery today indicates that the Government
need not have been too worried about hearing the original submissions on the bill at the
committee in public. I do not think the committee would have been overrun by unruly
behaviour. In fact, there would have been a transparent process that would give some of
the critics of the legislation some conf idence that nothing untoward was going on
through this bill.
I will focus on, and ask the Mini ster in the chair, the Atto rney-General, to address,
clause 5A of the bill. It is a matter that I referred to in my contribution on the first
reading of the bill, which is the drafting relating to proposed new section 4AAA(2),
inserted by clause 5A. Section 4AAA(1) was inserted into the bill at the
recommendation of the committee upon the submissions of, amongst others, the Human
Rights Commission. It makes it clear that in performing its functions under the New
Zealand Security Intelligence Service Act, the Security Intelligence Service: “(a)
contributes to keeping New Zealand so ciety secure, independent, and free and
democratic: (b) contributes to the participation of New Zealand in the maintenance of
international security: (c)”—this is more relevant to the question I am coming to—
“acts—(i) in accordance with New Zealand law and all human rights standards
recognised by New Zealand law, except to the extent that they are, in relation to
national security, modified by an enactment: (ii) in the discharge of its operational
functions, independently and impartially: (iii) with integrity and professionalism: (iv) in
a manner that facilitates effective democratic oversight.”
It is a wise addition to set out some principles that unde rlie the performance of the
Security Intelligence Service, but I just wonder whether the wording of subsection (2) is
so broad as to render nugatory subsection (1). Subsection (2) goes on to state:
“Subsection (1) does not impose particular dut ies on, or give particular powers to, the
Security Intelligence Service, the Direct or, any employee of the Service, or the
Minister.” So my question for the Minister—and the officials whom we seem to have in
the Chamber in support of the Minister seem to be rather secret at the moment—

items.text: Can’t you seem them?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I cannot see them, no.

items.text: Well, secret service powers ar e obviously being used. This
must be some device that has come from e ither KAOS or the other side. The Cone of
Silence does not seem to be working today, but the invisibility cloak is.
It rests upon the Minister, th en, to address this issue himself and to  explain how
subsection (2) does not make a complete nonsense of the very fine sentiments expressed
in subsection (1). I ask the Minister to explain how subsection (1) does not impose any
particular duties or give particular powers. I am not too worried a bout the powers; I am
worried about whether it imposes particular duties on the “Security Intelligence Service,
the Director, any employee of the Service, or  the Minister” and what that means. If it
means that there are some general duties or general obligations to comply with these
laws that are referred to and that act in accordance with New Zealand—

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I understand that there might not be any standard
over and above what is set out in those laws that has to be recognised or complied with

that subsection (1) states is that unless ther e is some modification in relation to national
security by some other enactment, then t hose other enactments apply anyway. So I do
not understand why we need s ubsection (2), and therefore I am confused by what it
means. Does it mean that no duties arise under  that Act? I thought that was one way we
might read it. I find it a surprising and conf using subsection, which I think makes this
legislation harder to interpret rather than easier.
I suggest to the Minister that he seek a dvice from officials as to whether we are
making things worse by that rather than better. If particular duties arise under those
statutes, well, they are not abrogated anyway. I presume that they are not intended to be
abrogated by new subsection (2). I am left c onfused as to what that subsection means. I
do not think it adds anything to the meaning of the statute, but, rather, it confuses
things.
I would be grateful if the Minister in th e chair addresses that issue when he has a
chance to consider it. It may well be that the officials, under their invisibility cloaks, are
considering this in some other part of the precinct, and maybe they need to come back
to him—

that if it does not require pa rticular duties, does it propose general duties, and, if they

items.text: One of the problems we have with discussing whether

items.text: Preventing thermonuclear war.

items.speaker: KEITH LOCKE
items.text: Well, it is interes ting that back in November 2009 there was a

items.text: He was a student at Victoria University who many years ago, and

protesting the Viet Nam War, apartheid, and the like. There was a huge furore about

Then the Ahmed Zaoui case came to public attention. The SIS claimed this as a great

items.text: It is relevant, particularly to the debate started up by David Parker
on clause 5A where it talks about the partic ular duties of the Security Intelligence

There was another big case where the Security Intelligence Service invaded the home

We can go back to an earlier case with  Dr William Ball Sutch, who was a leading
